newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan grain deal seeks to cut dependence on U.S..
newsitem.headline: Japan grain deal seeks to cut dependence on U.S..

text.p: A recent grain deal between a powerful Japanese farm cooperative and Australia's grain exporter signals Japan's eagerness to reduce its dependence on U.S. grain supplies, Japanese officials said on Wednesday.

The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) said on Tuesday that it and Japan's National Federation of Agricultural Co-Operative Associations (Zennoh) had established a joint venture in Tokyo, AWB-Zennoh Ltd, to trade feedgrains.
Zennoh is Japan's largest compound feed manufacturer, with annual turnover of nearly six trillion yen.
"Japan's dependence on the United States is increasing at a time when tight supply-demand conditions are expected in the world grain market, particularly in Asia," a senior Zennoh official said.
"We've considered shifting partly to Argentina and China for feed grain supplies, but Argentina exports grains mainly to Europe, while China lacks credibility as a stable supplier," he said.
"Australia is at least better than the others," he said.
After China banned corn exports in late 1994, Japan was forced to buy more U.S. corn, which led to an unusually high level of dependence on that country, industry officials said.
More than 98 percent of Japan's nearly 11.45 million tonnes of feed corn imports last year came from the United States, according to Finance Ministry data.

Last November, Japan's major trade houses and feed makers sent a mission to Argentina with the aim of boosting feed corn imports from that country, in order to diversify supply sources. In Japan, corn is used mainly to make feed.
AWB-Zennoh Ltd was capitalised at 30 million yen, with AWB holding a 51 percent share and Zennoh the remainder.
The venture's primary function will be to import Australian sorghum for use as feed grain, Zennoh officials said.
Japan imported about 2.19 million tonnes of sorghum in 1996, of which 483,874 tonnes came from Australia, according to Finance Ministry data.
Japanese traders echoed the view that Japan should diversify its grain suppliers, but warned there were potential pitfalls with the Australia deal as well.
"It's natural to diversify supply sources, but Australia's sorghum export capacity varies from year to year, because of drought for example," said a corn trader at a major Japanese trade house.
"Australia may be a good partner, but not the best one," he said.
